dataset.name: Carbonyl sulfide fluxes and concentrations from midwestern US (Bondville, FermiLab and Chicago)
description: This data package includes measurements of carbonyl sulfide (OCS) fluxes and concentrations from flux towers in the midwestern US. The measurements were made at AmeriFlux towers and thus the data package also includes a subset of the standard eddy covariance and meteorological data (e.g. VPD and NEE) that are also available from the AmeriFlux portal. The measurements presented here were made to provide an independent constraint on whole ecosystem stomatal conductance from these ecosystems with the goal of testing how the relationship between gross primary production and stomatal conductance varies through the growing season. Furthermore, we derived whole canopy nighttime stomatal conductance estimates to test how stomatal conductance varies between native prairie and maize ecosystems. All data presented here were discussed in the publication "Seasonal evolution of canopy stomatal conductance for a prairie and maize field in the midwestern US from continuous carbonyl sulfide fluxes" in Geophysical Research Letters (doi: 10.1029/2019GL085652).

measurementTechnique:
Sites and Field Deployment:
The measurements reported here were made at the Fermilab (41.8406N, -88.241W; 226.5 m above sea level), Bondville (40.0062N, -88.2904W; 219 m above sea level) and nearby Energy Farm (40.062359N, -88.195171W; 221 m above sea level) eddy covariance sites. The analysis at FermiLab was conducted nearly continuously over the 2016 and 2017 growing seasons and the data at the Bondville and Energy Farm sites was gathered during week-long campaigns during July and September 2015. At each site, the same Los Gatos Research Enhanced Performance Carbonyl Sulfide analyzer was installed at the base of the EC tower and measured concentrations of OCS, CO2, CO and H2O at 1 Hz frequency. Gas was sampled at four heights (4.4 m, 2.2 m, 1.2 m, and 0.32 m) using 1/4'' OD teflon lines with a PTFE filter. The lines were pumped at a constant flow rate of 10 L min-1 to ensure air was never stagnant in the lines and to minimize signal decay. The four lines were each sampled for 7 minutes to generate a profile every 30 minutes. We removed the first 3 minutes of sampling from each line to flush air from the cavity in the solenoid. The laser spectrometer was calibrated using a reference tank from NOAA GMD that was calibrated for CO (165.8 nmol mol-1), OCS (315.7 pmol mol-1) and CO2 (403.14 umol mol-). The repeat measurements of the calibration gas were used to apply a modest drift correction to the measured concentration of the gases.

Flux estimates:
To estimate the carbonyl sulfide flux, we used the flux gradient approach where:
OCS flux=Delta OCS/Delta CO2*NEE
where Delta OCS and Delta CO2 are the above canopy gradients derived from the OCS analyzer and NEE is the net ecosystem exchange of CO2 derived from the eddy covariance system. From this equation, we generated a 30-minute flux on the same timescale as the EC data and used the sign convention where flux towards the surface is positive. The measured OCS flux includes both vegetation and soil components, the latter of which was subtracted from the whole ecosystem flux to derive stomatal conductance. To estimate the soil flux, we collected soil samples through the growing season and conducted a series of flow-through incubations experiments to test the response of the OCS flux to temperature. Briefly, soils were stored frozen and then added to a darkened temperature-controlled chamber where air with ambient OCS concentrations and 100% relative humidity (to cease evaporation) was passed through the chamber with a fixed flow rate. We measured the OCS concentration of the air entering and exiting then chamber and used this to estimate the flux. We modeled the flux as a function of soil temperature and used this model to estimate the 30 minute soil OCS flux.
To estimate stomatal conductance (gs) from the OCS flux, we used the following set of equations:
total conductance=OCS flux/OCS concentration
and
total conductance=[boundary layer conductance^-1+stomatal conductance^-1+mesophyll conductance^-1+carbonic anhydrase conductance^-1]^-1
The stomatal conductance was then calculated as the component of the total conductance not accounted for by modeled estimates of the mesophyll, carbonic anhydrase, and boundary and components.
Lastly, we utilized the gs estimates along with canopy VPD to calculate transpiration and then we derived the transpiration fraction by dividing this number by ET from the EC data.

Ancillary data and flux filtering:
To estimate the ecosystem GPP for each site, we utilized the REddyProc R-package and partitioned NEE based on the "daytime method". We applied standard U* filtering to remove periods of high boundary layer stability. The approach requires inputs of NEE, latent heat flux, sensible heat flux, photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), VPD, air temperature, soil temperature and U*, which were all taken directly from the filtered EC data from each site.
Lastly, to generate a more complete annual cycle in OCS concentrations, we used OCS data collected during the winter of 2019 from the EPA AQS site #17-031-4002 in Chicago (41.751527N, -87.713437W). The data were collected using the same OCS analyzer and approach as the other sites.
